changes.before: Low-Voltage GaN Utilization for High-Voltage Stacked Polyphase Bridge Traction Drives
changes.after: Low-Voltage GaN Utilization in High-Voltage Stacked Polyphase Bridge Inverters for Truck Propulsion

changes.before: Abstract—The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) partitions a high-voltage traction dc link among series-connected submodules, enabling the use of low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) devices. Retaining their loss advantages at traction current requires sufficient drain- and gate-voltage margins in the physical building block. This paper evaluates a phase leg for a 300-kW, 1200-V drive, starting with a charge-based device comparison and a preliminary four-device parallel arrangement using the 100-V EPC2361. A KiCad–Ansys Q3D–LTspice workflow connects the routed prototype to a coupled parasitic network. Despite an estimated local commutation-loop inductance of 0.41 nH, the simulated voltage margin depends on gate-loop inductance, drive settings, and operating current. With a 10-nH gate loop and revised drive settings, sampled positive-current points from 1 A to 322 A remain below the 90-V drain–source target at a 75-V local bus; a 5% bus increase exceeds that target at rated current. The contribution is a quantified assessment of how implementation constraints feed back into SPB voltage partitioning. Experimental validation of one building block is planned for the full paper.
changes.after: Abstract—The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) partitions a high-voltage dc link for truck propulsion among series-connected submodules, enabling the use of low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) devices. Retaining their loss advantages at the required phase current requires sufficient drain- and gate-voltage margins in the physical building block. This paper evaluates a phase leg for a 300-kW, 1200-V truck propulsion system, starting with a charge-based device comparison and a preliminary four-device parallel arrangement using the 100-V EPC2361. A KiCad–Ansys Q3D–LTspice workflow connects the routed prototype to a coupled parasitic network. Despite an estimated local commutation-loop inductance of 0.41 nH, the simulated voltage margin depends on gate-loop inductance, drive settings, and operating current. With a 10-nH gate loop and revised drive settings, sampled positive-current points from 1 A to 322 A remain below the 90-V drain–source target at a 75-V local bus; a 5% bus increase exceeds that target at rated current. The contribution is a quantified assessment of how implementation constraints feed back into SPB voltage partitioning. Experimental validation of one building block is planned for the full paper.

changes.before: High dc-link voltages support traction power levels of several hundred kilowatts while requiring substantial phase current [1]. In a conventional two-level bridge, the switches block the full dc-link voltage. The stacked polyphase bridge (SPB) instead connects three-phase bridges in series on the dc side, each supplying an isolated winding set of a common machine [2], [3]. With suitable bypass hardware and winding control, its modular structure can support operation after a submodule fault at reduced capability. This benefit is conditional on the remaining submodules’ voltage and current margins; bypass operation is not evaluated here. Fig. 1 shows the topology and the building block considered.

changes.before: Voltage partitioning enables each SPB submodule to use a lower semiconductor voltage class, creating an opportunity to exploit the favorable on-state resistance and switching characteristics of low-voltage gallium nitride (GaN) devices in high-voltage traction drives [4]. Increasing the submodule count reduces the voltage across each bridge but leaves the phase-current requirement unchanged for fixed total power, dc-link voltage, modulation index, and power factor. Several devices may therefore be required in parallel, making current sharing, gate-drive impedance, and commutation paths central to realizing the expected device benefits.
